text:
[h1]True autonomy in Night City[/h1]

[b]Cyberpunk 2077[/b] completely blew me away because it flips the classic [i]"die young in a flash of glory"[/i] trope on its head—it’s a deeply personal story about [b]true autonomy[/b], surviving on your own terms, and facing the heavy weight of your choices without relying on cheap fairy-tale endings. The whole narrative framework kept me totally hooked, but what really sealed the deal was the core gameplay loop. 

Building out your V is insanely fun, and hands down, my favorite setup was my very first run: a [u]lethal stealth build[/u] pairing [b]high-damage revolvers with snipers[/b]. Cleaning out entire rooms from the shadows was just ridiculously satisfying. My only real gripe is how the game almost forces you to start a whole new playthrough from scratch just to experience different story branches and get full replayability, but as a complete package, it's easily one of the most compelling gaming experiences out there.

text:
The work of CD Projekt RED is more than just another AAA release that had to claw its way through a sea of bugs, complaints, and shattered expectations Every hour I spent with it felt like witnessing a romance come to life on my monitor - a cinematic tapestry woven from neon, cynicism, and a profound, piercing melancholy.

Ironically, my introduction to Night City was anything but conventional. I had certainly heard of the project, but I never felt any real desire to play it, perhaps due to my own peculiar take on sci-fi, both in video games and in cinema as well. A friend, however, kept urging me to at least give it a try - he was completely obsessed with this world, spending weeks on end raving about it and bombarding me with quotes and spoilers. I, for my part, kept brushing him off, shaking my head in skepticism. I assumed that beneath the flashy exterior, there was nothing substantial enough to truly hook me. As it turns out, I was totally wrong. Jesus of Christ.. Once I finally launched the game, the neon drenched Night City pulled me in completely, leaving me with a bittersweet realization of just how long I had resisted the inevitable.
Of course there is more to be said. The city itself is a fully developed character, depicted with a startlingly visceral and authentic detail. Night City is the dark that Philip K. D. forewarned us about, but it also bears the rain drenched noir sensibilities of Ridley Scott and even manages to emit a fine layer of satire that would make the best of dystopian fiction proud. It is a place in which glass towers are entwined into the singularity of a monument to human egoism that looms over slum streets, a place you walk down in downpour soaked streets or find yourself staring into the depths of neon lights only to realize that what you gaze upon is not a mere setting, but a monument to the world of late stage capitalism.

Each district possesses its own distinct aesthetic, in some places, the squalor of the slums sits side by si

This game taught me the difference between the minimum and recommended hardware steam gives you and the actual minimum and required hardware you need to run the game.

Yes, it ran like a baby with broken legs, but if i can get to level 120 at 576p and 18 fps then i see no reason for anyone to complain about this game being too demanding for their computers. That said, it really is demanding on your hardware and there is a reason I wouldn't recommend anyone else do what I did and may continue to do.

As for the gameplay, if you're looking to buy, prepare to get your balls crushed thoroughly. It's hard with a team and it's harder if you play solo, especially on the higher difficulties.

Also, the studio has a habit of making the game worse for no good reason, and not even putting said changes in the patch notes, so be aware of that as well.
